title: Our Children, Our Future: Tackling Child Poverty
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Reflecting on Labour's new Child Poverty Strategy, Hughes writes from lived experience of childhood hunger, ill-fitting clothes and hidden shame, describing how survival crowded out concentration and how she pretended concentration problems were laziness rather than admit their true cause. She argues the strategy matters because it acknowledges what schools cannot fix alone: many are already functioning as food banks and crisis centres while leaders in disadvantaged communities like her own in Merseyside 'are on their knees'. She frames measures like free school meals and breakfast clubs as necessary but insufficient without wider societal responsibility, arguing the strategy signals that lifting children from poverty 'belongs to the whole of society', not just overloaded headteachers and teachers. The piece closes on her own trajectory from poverty to professorship, framed as evidence of what becomes possible when a child's circumstances are met with both support and belief.
points: Hughes writes from first-person lived experience of childhood poverty - hunger blurring lessons, hiding in bathrooms to avoid mockery - grounding a policy analysis in testimony rather than abstraction.
Her claim that schools are 'already functioning as food banks, clothing banks, crisis centres and counselling hubs' names a specific, concrete burden being placed on an already stretched workforce.

She frames the Child Poverty Strategy's significance not as solving poverty through schools but as an acknowledgment that responsibility 'belongs to the whole of society', reframing schools' role in the poverty debate.
Her closing autobiographical arc - from a hungry child hiding in bathrooms to a professor - functions as both personal testimony and an argument for what becomes possible with structural support.
quotes: I see the child I once was. Hungry. Cold. Wearing clothes that never quite fit and carrying shame like an extra layer on my skin.

I remember the way hunger made lessons blur together as though I were looking through a fog. I remember pretending that my concentration problems were laziness or disinterest because it felt less painful than admitting that they came from fear and exhaustion.
Many schools are already functioning as food banks, clothing banks, crisis centres and counselling hubs. Leaders in the most challenging communities are burning out at a shocking rate.
The Child Poverty Strategy is an acknowledgement that schools cannot do it all. It belongs to the whole of society. It belongs to every department of government and every layer of policy.

Today I am a professor. I carry that title with pride not because it elevates me but because it reminds me of the long journey from the girl who hid in classrooms to the woman who speaks to lecture theatres full of students.
